tldr: When using differentiable physics simulations for robotic manipulation optimization, non-deterministic GPU parallel reduction order can flip the sign of parameter gradients, and accumulating numerical noise over longer horizons can cause finite-difference gradient validation to completely break down.
hero_caption: The two physical experiments and their corresponding Material Point Method (MPM) simulations studied in this work. Top row: an elastoplastic clay-crushing task (derived from DPSI); bottom row: a granular scooping task with sand (derived from DDBot).
overview:
When robots manipulate deformable materials such as clay or sand, differentiable physics simulation has attracted immense attention because it allows direct optimization of robot motions and material parameters through simulation. The biggest appeal is using backpropagation through contact-rich, complex simulations to compute gradients efficiently. However, whether gradients computed through long time horizons and non-linear contact formulations are truly reliable from a numerical standpoint had not been thoroughly investigated.

To address this question, the authors thoroughly evaluated the internal numerical behavior of differentiable simulators using two benchmarks: elastoplastic crushing and granular scooping. They carefully analyzed how GPU parallel execution order in the Material Point Method (MPM), consistency between automatic differentiation (AD) and finite differences (FD), and the design of observation data and loss functions impact optimization.

Their findings reveal that tiny floating-point rounding errors caused by thread scheduling variations on the GPU amplify across simulation steps, reversing the sign of parameter update gradients. Furthermore, as the simulation horizon grows, the run-to-run variation across identical forward rollouts rapidly outpaces the loss change induced by parameter perturbations, causing the finite-difference checks commonly used for gradient validation to fail. This study provides practical insights and action guidelines for successfully applying differentiable physics to robotic optimization.
contributions: Identified that non-deterministic execution order in GPU many-to-one parallel reductions amplifies numerical errors and can reverse the sign of parameter gradients.
Introduced a reproducible, deterministic reduction method using fixed-point integer addition that achieves bit-exact gradient computation.
Quantified the breakdown mechanism of finite-difference (FD) checks for automatic differentiation over long simulation horizons caused by rising run-to-run numerical variation.
Demonstrated how particle/point cloud geometric loss formulations and particle densities significantly impact optimization convergence and solution quality.

sections.heading: Can we truly trust differentiable physics simulators in robotics?
sections.summary: While differentiable simulations are increasingly used for robotic manipulation of deformable and granular materials, the numerical reliability underlying these optimization loops has remained unexamined. This paper investigates numerical reliability across three aspects—parallel reduction order, finite-difference validity, and observation/loss design—using two representative MPM benchmarks.
sections.details:
In tasks like food processing, excavation, and laboratory automation, robots must manipulate deformable and granular materials characterized by complex physics such as friction, flow, and contact. Recently, researchers have increasingly made simulators differentiable to perform system identification, trajectory optimization, skill acquisition, and end-effector design.

These optimization techniques rely entirely on gradient signals propagated through long, contact-rich simulation rollouts. However, the question of how numerically accurate these gradients actually are has often been overlooked.

The Material Point Method (MPM) is a powerful approach for simulating large-deformation materials. It transfers momentum between particles (Lagrangian frame) and a background grid (Eulerian frame). During the particle-to-grid (P2G) transfer and throughout reverse-mode automatic differentiation, many-to-one parallel reductions (accumulating many particle contributions onto a single grid node) occur frequently.

Because standard atomic additions on GPUs do not guarantee thread completion order, floating-point rounding errors introduce slight discrepancies depending on execution order. Building on prior literature, the authors set out to determine how severely these computational errors affect long-horizon gradient computation using two controlled tasks: clay crushing (derived from DPSI) and sand scooping (derived from DDBot).

sections.heading: The experimental setup and protocols for dissecting numerical reliability
sections.summary: Using two benchmarks covering elastoplastic and granular materials, the authors established a systematic testing protocol with a unified contact model to examine numerical precision, horizon lengths, and observation formulations. They also introduced a deterministic fixed-point integer reduction method to eliminate GPU non-determinism.
sections.details:
### II-A Benchmark Setup
The study uses two configurations with distinct material properties. The first is an elastoplastic model derived from DPSI (using fixed corotational elasticity and von Mises yield criterion), and the second is a granular model derived from DDBot (using Hencky / Saint-Venant–Kirchhoff elasticity and Drucker–Prager yield criterion). To eliminate discrepancies caused by different contact treatments, both setups employ the same signed distance field (SDF)-based projective contact model.

Testing conditions comprehensively covered single precision (f32) vs. double precision (f64), multiple geometric loss functions (Chamfer Distance: CD, Earth Mover's Distance: EMD, and Height Map Distance: HMD), varying particle densities, and different simulation horizon lengths. Observations were structured into two pipelines: direct particle comparisons (PRT) and surface point cloud comparisons (PCD).

### II-B Gradient Evaluation and Deterministic Accumulation
To validate the correctness of gradients computed by automatic differentiation (AD), the authors compared them against central finite differences (FD) computed by perturbing parameters by a small step $h$. Crucially, they measured the ratio between the perturbation-induced loss change $\Delta L_{\theta}(h)$ and the repeated-run loss variation $V$ from identical simulations without parameter perturbations. If the variation $V$ is too large, the finite-difference estimate itself is drowned out by numerical noise.

To resolve thread scheduling non-determinism from atomic additions on the GPU, they implemented a deterministic reduction that quantizes floating-point values into a shared fixed-point integer scale for integer addition. This guarantees complete bit-level reproducibility regardless of thread arrival order, isolating error propagation.

sections.heading: Three surprising findings revealed by the experiments
sections.summary: Non-deterministic GPU reduction order reversed the algebraic sign of a parameter gradient. As rollout horizons grew, exploding numerical noise rendered finite-difference checks useless. Furthermore, choices in loss function design and observation resolution substantially distorted optimization outcomes.
sections.details:
### III-A Parallel Reductions Can Reverse Backpropagation Gradients
Using standard additions on the GPU produces tiny discrepancies on the order of $10^{-7}$ (f32) or $10^{-16}$ (f64) as early as the first P2G step. These errors amplify exponentially as they propagate backward through long reverse-mode AD computation graphs.

In a 311-step granular scooping rollout, the single-threaded deterministic CPU reference gradient for Poisson's ratio $\partial L/\partial\nu$ was $-7.99$. In contrast, the ensemble mean from standard GPU runs was $+1.29$—the gradient sign completely reversed. Following this simulator gradient would drive parameter updates in the exact opposite direction of the ground truth. When the deterministic fixed-point reduction was introduced, bit-exact agreement was confirmed across all five representative test configurations.

### III-B Finite-Difference Checks Break Down over Longer Horizons
Finite-difference (FD) checks are standard for verifying gradient implementations, but they become unreliable as rollouts lengthen. At 2 steps in the elastoplastic model, the perturbation-induced loss change $\Delta L_{\theta}(h)$ was 93 to 806 times larger than run-to-run variation $V$, yielding a clear signal. However, beyond 10 steps, this ratio plummeted to only 2 to 14. Numerical noise across identical runs grew far faster than the true effect of parameter perturbations.

Even with double precision (f64), finite differences failed to converge at 20 and 40 steps, and the relative error against AD spiked up to $3.41\times 10^{-1}$ (about 34%). This highlights the danger of treating finite differences as an unquestioned ground-truth baseline in long-horizon simulations.

### III-C Observation and Loss Formulation Dictate Optimization
Optimization behavior depends heavily on geometric loss formulation, not just physical laws. Particle-based Chamfer Distance (PRT-CD) steadily decreased its own loss across 97.5% of tested epochs. However, when evaluating the final reconstructed geometry against an independent external metric (Height Map Distance, HMD), PRT-EMD—which only decreased its own loss in 67.5% of epochs—produced superior geometric recovery. This is a classic case where the optimized objective does not align with true geometric fidelity.

Moreover, quadrupling the simulation particle count from 218 to 876 only increased the observed surface cell count from 89 to 151 (a 1.7× increase). Increasing simulation resolution does not proportionally scale observation resolution, showing that discretization design directly dictates gradient information.

sections.heading: Three practical guidelines for using differentiable physics properly
sections.summary: Based on their findings, the authors propose concrete best practices for applying differentiable physics to system identification, trajectory optimization, and robot design. They emphasize reproducible accumulation, noise-aware FD validation, and explicit reporting of observation pipelines.
sections.details:
The insights from this paper apply beyond system identification to any robotics research integrating physics engines into optimization loops—including contact-rich trajectory optimization, policy learning, and differentiable end-effector design. The authors recommend three practical guidelines:

- **Adopt reproducible accumulation methods**: To prevent small rounding errors from amplifying across long horizons, deterministic reductions (such as fixed-point accumulation) should be used for gradient-affecting many-to-one parallel reductions.
- **Conduct noise-aware finite-difference checks**: When validating automatic differentiation (AD) with finite differences (FD), researchers should not merely test multiple perturbation sizes $h$, but also measure repeated-run variation $V$ without perturbations to verify that $\Delta L_{\theta}(h) \gg V$. If finite differences do not converge as $h$ decreases, that FD check cannot serve as a reliable reference.
- **Report observation and discretization pipelines in detail**: Geometric loss formulations, point cloud sampling methods, and surface extraction algorithms heavily influence optimization gradients. These should be treated as essential problem specifications and reported explicitly to ensure reproducibility.

While this study focused on a Taichi-based MPM implementation and two specific manipulation motions, it marks an important milestone warning against treating differentiable simulators as black boxes.

sections.heading: Appendix: MPM formulation, checkpointing, and fixed-point addition details
sections.summary: The appendix details the MPM algorithm, memory reduction via checkpointing, custom SVD derivatives, mathematical formulations for fixed-point integer reproducibility, and comprehensive experimental data.
sections.details:
### A MPM Formulation and Observation Operators
The simulation is based on Moving Least Squares MPM (MLS-MPM) with Affine Particle-In-Cell (APIC). Each substep follows a dataflow of Particle-to-Grid transfer (P2G), grid-based contact and external force updates, and Grid-to-Particle interpolation (G2P). Both P2G and the adjoint G2P calculations in reverse-mode AD feature many-to-one reductions onto shared grid nodes.

### B Reverse-Mode AD and Deterministic Fixed-Point Accumulation
Storing the computation graph for long rollouts quickly exhausts memory, so checkpointing across time windows $W$ is used to recompute required forward states on the fly. Grid fields accounted for 99.4% of the memory footprint. Because the environment lacked native AD support for Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), the vector-Jacobian products for SVD in the constitutive models were implemented manually.

For deterministic reduction, each floating-point contribution $c_i$ is quantized using a shared fractional bit width $F$ as $q_i = \mathrm{round}(c_i \cdot 2^F)$. Because integer addition is strictly associative, the sum is unique regardless of GPU thread completion order. To prevent overflow, a split double-word representation (high and low fields) was implemented.

### C Detailed Experimental Results and Computational Overhead
Executing SDF contact computation entirely on the GPU eliminated CPU-GPU data transfers, yielding a 92.9× speedup for contact calculation alone and a 12.73× overall speedup. Furthermore, the fixed-point accumulator not only guaranteed exact reproducibility, but also preserved higher accuracy (error of $2.00\times 10^{-10}$) than the best-case non-deterministic floating-point atomic run (error of $1.44\times 10^{-9}$).

takeaways: Thread scheduling non-determinism in GPU atomic additions can accumulate over long differentiable simulation horizons to the point of flipping the algebraic sign of parameter gradients.

Finite-difference (FD) checks are not an infallible ground truth; over longer rollout horizons, numerical noise from repeated identical runs can drown out the perturbation signal and invalidate the check.
Minimizing surface loss functions like Chamfer Distance does not guarantee recovery of true geometry when evaluated against independent external metrics.

Increasing simulation particle resolution does not proportionally improve the resolution of observed surface point clouds; physical and observational discretization should be designed and reported separately.
limitations: The empirical evaluation is limited to an MPM simulator implemented in the Taichi language; testing across other differentiable engines (e.g., Warp, Brax, Genesis) and finite element methods (FEM) remains future work.
The benchmarks are restricted to two specific manipulation scenarios: elastoplastic clay crushing and granular sand scooping.
The proposed deterministic fixed-point reduction introduces integer conversion overhead and requires expanded memory representations (split high/low word fields).
